The link has accessible name "HTML" and is alone in its enclosing block. The name "HTML" is a format-only token that doesn't identify what document/resource the link points to. The surrounding region shows "Ulys" and "HTML EPUB" suggesting this is part of a list of download formats for some content, but the descriptive text naming the subject is in a separate sibling block, not enclosing the link.

This is a classic format-only name barrier: "HTML" alone doesn't tell you where the link goes or what it is for.

The link has accessible name "Plain text" and is alone in its enclosing block. The surrounding region shows "UB Plain text" which appears to be in a table context. The name "Plain text" is a format-only descriptor - it tells the user what format the content is in, but not what the content actually is (the destination/subject).

The link is alone in its cell, so the only programmatic context is its own name. "Plain text" is a format-only name that doesn't identify the destination subject. This is a 2.4.4 barrier.

Wait, but looking at the surrounding region, I can see "Ulysses" above and "UB Plain text" - this appears to be a table where "Ulysses" is the row header and "Plain text" is a link in that row. 

But sibling data cells don't provide enclosing context for the link itself - only the cell it's in matters. Since the link stands alone in its cell with just "Plain text" as its accessible name, and that's purely format-based without indicating where the link goes, this is definitely a 2.4.4 barrier.

Let me analyze this link. The accessible name is "HTML" and the enclosing context block text is "Ulysses". 

The link text is "HTML" and it's within a list item that contains "Ulysses" as the enclosing block text. Looking at the surrounding region, I can see "Ulysses" as a parent item, and "HTML" and "EPUB" as sub-list items.

The question is: does "HTML" alone or with its context ("Ulysses") identify the link purpose?
Since the link sits within a block containing "Ulysses" and isn't the only element in that block, the enclosing context provides necessary information. Together, "Ulysses HTML" clearly identifies the purpose—it's a link to the HTML version of the book. That's sufficient to determine what the link does. So "Ulysses" is indeed part of the enclosing block context for the "HTML" link, meaning the link's purpose is determinable from the combination of the format name and the work name together. This isn't a barrier to accessibility—the context is sufficient for users to understand they're getting the HTML version of Ulysses.

The link has accessible name "EPUB" and the enclosing block text is "Ulysses". The link sits in a list item that contains "EPUB" as a link, and the surrounding region shows a list with HTML, EPUB, Plain text links. The enclosing context shows "Ulysses" as the block text.

So the link is "EPUB" within a list item that is nested under "Ulysses". The enclosing list item context includes "Ulysses" which is the title/subject. So the link purpose is: download/access Ulysses in EPUB format.
The combination of "Ulysses" as the enclosing context and "EPUB" as the link name clearly identifies the purpose. Looking at the DOM structure, the nested list sits inside the parent list item, with the EPUB link positioned as the second item in that nested list. The combination of the work title and format option is sufficient to convey the link's purpose without needing additional context.

The link has accessible name "Plain text" and sits in a list with other format links (HTML, EPUB, Plain text). The enclosing block text is "Ulysses" - meaning the list item or its parent contains "Ulysses" as context.

So the link purpose is: download/access "Ulysses" in Plain text format. The name "Plain text" is a format-only name, but the enclosing context "Ulysses" names the subject. Together, name+context = "Plain text version of Ulysses" which is determinable.
The context "Ulysses" fully clarifies what the format-only name refers to, so this isn't an accessibility barrier.

The link has accessible name "Workshop" and is alone in its enclosing block. The name "Workshop" is not a generic action word like "click here" or "read more" - it actually names something specific (a Workshop). Let me consider whether "Workshop" alone is sufficient to identify the link's purpose.

"Workshop" is a descriptive word that names the destination/content. It's not a bare action word or format-only name. It tells the user they'll go to a Workshop page/resource. While it's somewhat vague (what workshop?), it's more specific than "click here" or "read more."

However, looking at the surrounding region, I can see text "The W3C held a" followed by "Workshop" as a link. 

Since the link is alone in its enclosing block, the preceding text "The W3C held a" isn't part of the same block context. So I need to evaluate whether "Workshop" standing by itself provides enough information about the link's purpose - it names the destination but lacks context about what kind of workshop or why it matters.

The real question is whether "Workshop" is too generic or if it's specific enough in this W3C context. I should check if there are other links with the same name on the page, since identical link text pointing to different destinations would be a problem. To determine if this link passes WCAG standards, I need to figure out whether "Workshop" alone is specific enough to identify its destination. A screen reader user encountering just the word "Workshop" should be able to tell where it leads—and since it's a proper noun naming a specific thing rather than a generic action word, it likely does meet the requirement. I don't see other same-named links pointing elsewhere, so I'll conclude this isn't a barrier.

Looking at the evidence:

- **Accessible name:** "Workshop"
- **Enclosing block:** Link is alone in its block; the text "The W3C held a" is a *preceding sibling*, not an enclosing ancestor — it does not count as programmatic context.
- **Name alone:** "Workshop" is a specific noun naming a destination. It is not a generic action word ("click here," "read more," "more," "details") nor a format-only token ("PDF," "DOCX"). It identifies the linked resource as a workshop.

"Workshop" names the destination content type with enough specificity to distinguish it from other link purposes. It is not in the class of opaque names WCAG 2.4.4 targets.
